selectionReason: First choice kept: Ras Mohammed has a recent open-access, park-specific study of visitor pressure on its reefs (2023), plus 2022–2026 GEF/UNDP project documents and an IUCN Green List record, and its Bedouin tourism concession and dive-tourism economy make it directly relevant to regenerative tourism enterprises.

overview.text: Declared a protected area in 1983 (Decree No. 1068), the park lies at the southern tip of Sinai, about 12 km from Sharm El-Sheikh, and covers land and sea; reported areas differ between sources (460 km² to 850 km²).
The Nature Conservation Sector of the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency (EEAA) is responsible for managing Egypt's protected areas, including Ras Mohammed.

In November 2018 it became the first marine protected area in Africa and the Middle East to receive IUCN Green List certification; monitoring cited by IUCN found average live coral cover above 65%, against 20–30% typical outside the reserve.

livelihoods.text: The local Bedouin community holds an exclusive tourism concession in the park; land-based tourism, some boat tours and all camping are managed by the Bedouin community under it.
The park has hired Bedouin as skippers and community guards, and a GEF/UNDP project built shaded pavilions where local Bedouin groups sell food and other products to visitors.
When COVID-19 halted park tourism in 2020, hundreds of local tourism workers such as guides, drivers and boat captains lost their jobs, and local women who make handicrafts lost their income.

challenges.title: Heavy diving and snorkelling pressure on the reefs

statements.text: Visits rose from 77,550 in 1994/95 to 520,012 in 2009/10 and were 444,653 in 2018/19, mostly people who snorkel or dive on the reefs.

Citing earlier studies, a 2023 review reports that the six most-visited dive sites receive over 70,000 divers a year, and that broken corals were far more common at sites open to divers (8.2%) than at closed sites (0.6–1.2%).
The same review concludes that current management frameworks seem insufficient to cope with rising visitation.

The Green Sharm El Sheikh project rates as high the risk that protection of the marine protected areas near Sharm El-Sheikh, including Ras Mohamed, is undermined by tourism growth and fishing pressure.

challenges.title: Resort growth, boat traffic and fishing pressure from Sharm El-Sheikh

statements.text: Sharm El-Sheikh's development now runs along the shore from the park's northern edge to Nabq; hotel rooms grew from 515 in 1988 to 51,695 in 2016, and diving boats from 26 to about 300.
Illegal fishing and rising demand for seafood from Sharm El-Sheikh's residents and restaurants have affected several reef fisheries.
Policies of the institutions developing tourism occasionally clash with the park's conservation strategies.
Entrance and camping fees were significant sources of the park's budget and were lost when protected areas closed to visitors from March to June 2020.
The Green Sharm project's baseline puts the combined average annual budget of the three South Sinai protected areas (Ras Mohamed, Nabq and Abu Galum) at USD 75,000.
The project's 2023 environmental and social assessment states that total financing for the South Sinai protected-area system is still insufficient and that some areas face a serious shortage.

opportunities.title: Bedouin-run, lower-volume visitor services

rationale.text: Bedouin already run land tourism, some boat tours and all camping in the park under an exclusive concession.
A GEF/UNDP project built pavilions at Ras Mohammed where Bedouin groups sell food and other products.
Visitors surveyed in an earlier study preferred less crowded sites in exchange for healthier reefs, and its scenario with 50% fewer visitors gave a higher net benefit than the status quo.
Growing Bedouin-run guided, camping, food and craft services that earn more per visitor could add local income and park revenue without adding more people to the reefs.

validationNeeded: What the concession allows, and who holds it now
Whether visitors on Sharm El-Sheikh package trips would pay for higher-value, less crowded visits
How much fee revenue the park keeps (the Green Sharm project plans new fee and permit systems)
Agreement from EEAA's Nature Conservation Sector

statement.text: Funded the 2010–2020 project that built visitor pavilions where Bedouin groups sell food and products at Ras Mohammed.
With the GEF, ran the 2010–2020 protected-area financing and management project that built visitor facilities at Ras Mohammed, including pavilions where Bedouin groups sell products.
As the park's managing authority it sets concession and visitor rules, so any new service would need its approval.

opportunities.title: Reef-etiquette briefing and guide training for dive and snorkel operators

rationale.text: Workshops and training have been organised for hotel staff, dive instructors and guides, and the park's rules distributed in several languages.
An earlier study at the park found that one briefing cut divers' contact with living coral from 0.9 to 0.15 times per diver per 7 minutes.

The Green Sharm project plans to identify best practices for Ras Mohamed and the other Sharm El-Sheikh protected areas (anchoring systems, carrying-capacity assessments, zoning) and to develop guidelines for diving and visits.
A local service that trains guides and gives standard briefings and in-water checks for operators could help these rules be followed at busy sites.

validationNeeded: Whether briefings are already compulsory and who delivers them
Whether operators would pay for training or checks
Fresh evidence on diver impacts (the briefing study dates from 1997)
Overlap with Green Sharm project and EEAA programmes

statement.text: Implements the Green Sharm El Sheikh project, which plans pilots, guidelines and training to manage tourism threats in Ras Mohamed and the nearby protected areas.
As the park's managing authority it sets diving rules and access, so a briefing or training service would need to fit its programme.

organisations.name: Nature Conservation Sector, Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency

role.text: Responsible for nature conservation and protected-area management in Egypt, including Ras Mohammed; a 2023 study of the park lists its measures, such as mooring buoys, walkways, a USD 5 daily user fee and a reef-damage fee.
GEF implementing agency for the 2010–2020 protected-area financing project and for the Green Sharm El Sheikh project (approved 2022), which supports improved management of Ras Mohamed.

Funded the 2010–2020 project that supported efforts to reduce tourism impacts on Ras Mohammed's reefs, coral monitoring in South Sinai and a new permit and concession system for protected areas, and funds the Green Sharm El Sheikh project.

organisations.name: International Union for Conservation of Nature

role.text: Awarded Ras Mohammed National Park IUCN Green List certification in November 2018 after an evaluation against 50 indicators.

verificationNote: All sources were fetched with curl and the facts checked in the fetched text (PDFs via pdftotext). The main park-specific source is Tawfik (2023, peer-reviewed, CC BY); many of its pressure figures come from studies of the 1990s–2000s, which the challenge statements present as cited evidence. Recent context comes from GEF/UNDP documents (2022 feature, 2022 CEO endorsement, 2023 ESIA; the 2026 mid-term review was read but reports no park-specific results) and IUCN (2018). Sources disagree on the park's area (460, 480 or 850 km²) and founding year (1983 decree vs 1986 in IUCN's story).
gaps: No recent (post-2018) field survey of reef condition at Ras Mohammed was found. HEPCA's 2023–2024 bleaching reports cover the whole Egyptian coast, are not park-specific and restrict reuse of their data, so they were not used.
The 2007 EEAA management-effectiveness evaluation and the undated draft park management plan were found, but were judged too old to cite for current conditions.
No current figure for the park's own budget, its staffing, or how much fee revenue it keeps was found.
The terms of the Bedouin tourism concession (holders, scope, revenue sharing) are not documented in the sources.
The Green Sharm mid-term review (March 2026) lists mooring buoys near coral reefs among co-financed results, but does not say whether any are in Ras Mohammed.
The mdpi.com page for Tawfik (2023) blocked automated access; the publisher's mirror PDF was used instead.
